subtopics.title: Classify numbers into sets
subtopics.exposition: Natural numbers, written N, are the set {1; 2; 3; ...}. Whole numbers, written N_0, are the set {0; 1; 2; 3; ...}. Integers, written Z, are the set {...; -3; -2; -1; 0; 1; 2; 3; ...}. The square root of a negative number is called a non-real or imaginary number. The square roots of -1, -28 and -5 are all non-real numbers.

subtopics.title: Identify rational and irrational numbers
subtopics.exposition: A rational number (Q) is any number which can be written as a/b, where a and b are integers and b is not equal to 0. 10/1, 21/7, -1/-3, 10/20 and -3/6 are examples of rational numbers. Irrational numbers (Q') are numbers that cannot be written as a fraction with the numerator and denominator as integers. The square root of 2, the square root of 3, the cube root of 4, pi, and (1 + the square root of 5)/2 are examples of irrational numbers. In each of the rational-number examples, all numerators and all denominators are integers. All integers are rational numbers, because they can be written with a denominator of 1. All integers, and all fractions with integer numerators and non-zero integer denominators, are rational numbers. Any rational number can be written as a decimal number, but not all decimal numbers are rational numbers. Decimal numbers that end (terminate) are rational numbers; for example the fraction 4/10 can be written as 0.4. Decimal numbers that have a repeating single digit are rational numbers; for example the fraction 1/3 can be written as 0.333... Decimal numbers that have a recurring pattern of multiple digits are rational numbers; for example the fraction 2/11 can be written as 0.181818... Irrational decimal numbers like the square root of 2 (1.4142135...) cannot be written with an integer numerator and denominator, because they do not have a pattern of recurring digits and they do not terminate. To identify whether a number is rational or irrational, first write the number in decimal form; if the number terminates then it is rational. If the decimal goes on forever, look for a repeated pattern of digits; if there is no repeated pattern, then the number is irrational. Worked example 1: pi and 1.618033989... are irrational because the decimal does not terminate and has no repeated pattern. Worked example 1: 1.4 is rational because its decimal terminates. Worked example 1: 1.7373737373... and 0,(bar over 02) are rational because their decimals have a repeated pattern. Irrational numbers written in decimal form can be continued for many decimal places, which is not convenient, so it is often necessary to round off.

subtopics.title: Use recurring decimal notation
subtopics.exposition: A dot or a bar over the repeated digits indicates that the decimal is a recurring decimal. If the bar covers more than one digit, then all the numbers beneath the bar are recurring. The dot and bar notations are equivalent: 0.3 with a dot, 0.3 with a bar and 0.333... all represent recurring 3's. The fraction 1/3 can be written as the decimal 0.3 with a dot over the 3 or 0.3 with a bar over the 3. A bar over a pattern of digits represents that pattern recurring; the bar over 18 means 0.181818... The fraction 2/11 can be written as the decimal 0,(bar over 18). A full stop may be used instead of a comma to indicate a decimal number, so 0.4 can also be written as 0.4.

subtopics.title: Convert terminating decimals to fractions
subtopics.exposition: A decimal number has an integer part and a fractional part. 10.589 has an integer part of 10 and a fractional part of 0.589, because 10 + 0.589 = 10.589. 0.1 is 1/10, 0.01 is 1/100 and 0.001 is 1/1000. Each digit after the decimal point is a fraction with a denominator in increasing powers of 10. To convert a terminating decimal to a fraction, write the integer part plus each digit after the decimal point over its power of 10: 10.589 = 10 + 5/10 + 8/100 + 9/1000. Rewrite each term over the common denominator 1000: 10 000/1000 + 500/1000 + 80/1000 + 9/1000. Add the fractions over the common denominator to get 10.589 = 10 589/1000.

subtopics.title: Convert recurring decimals to fractions
subtopics.exposition: If one digit is recurring, multiply by 10; if two digits are recurring, multiply by 100; if three digits are recurring, multiply by 1000, and so on. Step 1, define an equation: let x equal the recurring decimal, e.g. x = 0.33333... Step 2, multiply both sides by 10 (one digit recurring): 10x = 3.33333... Step 3, subtract the first equation from the second equation: 9x = 3. Step 4, simplify: x = 3/9 = 1/3. Step 1, define an equation: x = 5.432432432... Step 2, multiply both sides by 1000 (three digits recurring): 1000x = 5432.432432432... Step 3, subtract the first equation from the second equation: 999x = 5427. Step 4, simplify: x = 5427/999 = 201/37 = 5 16/37.
